title: Παρακαταθήκην εἰληφὼς καὶ Ὅρκος
titleEn: The Man Who Took a Deposit, and Oath
part: The Man Who Took a Deposit, and Oath (Chambry 298)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 298. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Παρακαταθήκην τις λαβὼν φίλου ἀποστερεῖν διενοεῖτο.
sentences.tr: Parakatathēkēn tis labōn philou aposterein dienoeito.
sentences.l: A certain man, having taken a deposit from a friend, was minded to defraud him of it.
sentences.n: παρακαταθήκη is money or goods left with another for safe keeping, and one the Greeks felt keenly, since nothing but the holder's honesty secured it; the moral of fable 229 turns on the same word and on the same verb ἀποστερέω. The genitive φίλου can hang either on the deposit ('a friend's deposit') or on ἀποστερεῖν, which takes the genitive of the person robbed; the sense comes out the same. A note on the number: Chambry's editio minor prints no fable numbered 298 — the numeral 299 stands over this fable and over the next one alike, a compositor's slip. This edition publishes the first of the pair as 298 and the second as 299; the Greek itself is untouched.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ προσκαλουμένου αὐτὸν ἐκείνου ἐπὶ ὅρκον, εὐλαβούμενος εἰς ἀγρὸν ἐπορεύετο.
sentences.tr: Kai dē proskaloumenou auton ekeinou epi horkon, eulaboumenos eis agron eporeueto.
sentences.l: And indeed, when that man summoned him to an oath, he, being wary, set out into the country.
sentences.n: Genitive absolute — the fable's ordinary way of setting the circumstance aside from the main verb, and it will recur here. Challenging a man to swear was the regular way of settling a dispute over a deposit, since there was no other proof; the challenge is what drives him out of town.

sentences.t: Γενόμενος δὲ κατὰ τὰς πύλας, ὡς ἐθεάσατό τινα χωλὸν ἐξιόντα, ἐπυνθάνετο αὐτοῦ τίς τε εἴη καὶ ποῖ πορεύοιτο.
sentences.tr: Genomenos de kata tas pylas, hōs etheasato tina chōlon exionta, epynthaneto autou tis te eiē kai poi poreuoito.
sentences.l: And having come to be at the gates, when he saw a certain lame man going out, he inquired of him who he was and whither he was going.
sentences.i: And when he reached the city gates and saw a lame man going out, he asked him who he was and where he was bound.
sentences.n: εἴη and πορεύοιτο are optatives of the indirect question in secondary sequence: the man's own words were 'who are you and where are you going?', and the optative marks them as reported. πυνθάνομαι takes the genitive of the person asked.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ εἰπόντος αὐτὸν Ὅρκον εἶναι καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς βαδίζειν, ἐκ δευτέρου ἠρώτα διὰ πόσου χρόνου ἐπιφοιτᾶν ταῖς πόλεσι εἴωθεν.
sentences.tr: Tou de eipontos auton Horkon einai kai epi tous asebeis badizein, ek deuterou ērōta dia posou chronou epiphoitan tais polesi eiōthen.
sentences.l: And when he said that he was Oath and was walking against the impious, a second time he asked at how long an interval of time he was accustomed to visit the cities.
sentences.i: And when he said that he was Oath, and was on his way against the impious, he asked him next at what intervals he was in the habit of visiting the cities.
sentences.n: Ὅρκος is the Oath itself, met on the road as a person: the divine power that pursues the man who swears falsely. His lameness is the traditional slow foot of divine punishment, and the fable is built to overturn it — the interval he names is long, and the ending is not. διὰ with the genitive of time measures the interval that passes between visits. εἴωθα is a perfect with present force, 'I am accustomed'.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἔφη· « Διὰ τεσσαράκοντα ἐτῶν, ἐνίοτε δὲ καὶ τριάκοντα. »
sentences.tr: Ho de ephē· « Dia tessarakonta etōn, eniote de kai triakonta. »
sentences.l: And he said: « At intervals of forty years, but sometimes even thirty. »

sentences.t: Καὶ ὃς οὐδὲν μελλήσας τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ ὤμοσε μὴ εἰληφέναι τὴν παρακαταθήκην.
sentences.tr: Kai hos ouden mellēsas tēi hysteraiāi ōmose mē eilēphenai tēn parakatathēkēn.
sentences.l: And he, having delayed not at all, on the next day swore that he had not received the deposit.
sentences.n: καὶ ὅς, 'and he', is the old demonstrative use of the word that elsewhere is a relative; it resumes the subject sharply, as at fable 229. μή, not οὐ, is the negative that goes with an infinitive after a verb of swearing.

sentences.t: Περιπεσὼν δὲ τῷ Ὅρκῳ, καὶ ἀπαγόμενος ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ κρημνόν, ᾐτιᾶτο αὐτὸν ὡς προειπὼν αὐτῷ διὰ τριάκοντα ἐτῶν ἐπιπορεύεσθαι, οὐδὲ πρὸς μίαν ἡμέραν ἄδειαν δέδωκεν.
sentences.tr: Peripesōn de tōi Horkōi, kai apagomenos hyp’ autou epi krēmnon, ēitiato auton hōs proeipōn autōi dia triakonta etōn epiporeuesthai, oude pros mian hēmeran adeian dedōken.
sentences.l: But having fallen in with Oath, and being led away by him to a cliff, he charged him with this, that though having said beforehand to him that he came round at intervals of thirty years, he had granted him immunity for not even one day.
sentences.i: But he fell in with Oath, and as he was being led off by him to a cliff he complained that Oath had told him beforehand he came round only every thirty years, and yet had allowed him not one day's grace.
sentences.n: The construction shifts in mid-sentence: ὡς προειπών sets up a participial charge, and then δέδωκεν, a finite perfect, takes over where a second participle was owed. Chambry prints it so; it is the loose syntax of the collection, not an error to be mended. ἄδεια is freedom from fear of punishment, a safe-conduct. περιπίπτω is to fall in with a thing by chance, and the chance is never good.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ὑπολαβὼν ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ εὖ ἴσθι ὡς, ὅταν μέλλῃ τις ἀνιᾶσαί με, καὶ αὐθημερὸν ἐπιφοιτᾶν εἴωθα. »
sentences.tr: Ho de hypolabōn ephē· « All’ eu isthi hōs, hotan mellēi tis aniasai me, kai authēmeron epiphoitan eiōtha. »
sentences.l: But he, taking-up-the-word, said: « Well, know well that, whenever someone means to vex me, I am accustomed to visit even on the same day. »
sentences.i: But Oath took him up and said: « Understand this: whenever a man sets out to vex me, I am in the habit of coming that very day. »
sentences.n: ὑπολαβών is 'taking up the word', the collection's word for a reply, not for any physical seizing. ἀνιάω is to grieve or vex. ὅταν with the subjunctive states what happens whenever the case arises.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι ἀδιόριστός ἐστιν ἡ κατὰ τῶν ἀσεβῶν ἐκ θεοῦ τιμωρία.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti adioristos estin hē kata tōn asebōn ek theou timōria.
sentences.l: The story shows that the punishment from god against the impious is not marked off to any fixed term.
sentences.n: ἀδιόριστος is 'not bounded off', with no determined limit — the whole force of the fable sits in the word, since the perjurer had counted on the interval. κατά with the genitive is 'down upon, against'.
